The lower two-wire section is about λ/4 long and helps match the radiator to a 50 Ω feedline. Moving the feed taps changes the input impedance.

Enter the frequency you want to tune the antenna to. The default is 146.000 MHz.
The shortening factor k adjusts the radiator and matching stub lengths. A value of 0.95 makes their calculated lengths 5% shorter.
These formulas give starting dimensions. Check geometry and matching on the assembled antenna.
Enter f in MHz. Lengths are in metres.
Centre-to-centre spacing S ≈ (0.01–0.03)λ. The reference example uses S = 0.025λ.
Starting feed tap height h ≈ 0.022λ (A in the drawing). Refine the position using SWR and impedance measurements.
The shortening factor k depends on the geometry. The reference example uses k ≈ 0.95 for 12–15 mm copper pipe and k ≈ 0.97 for thin wire. Twin-lead designs use their own dimensions.
Wavelength is in metres and antenna dimensions are in millimetres. On narrow screens, scroll sideways to see all columns.
A separate 2 m example for 145.000 MHz. The dimensions below are starting values for the copper build.

Copper pipe with a 12–15 mm outside diameter, two 90° elbows, a short piece for the shorting bar, a cap for the short element, an SO-239 or N connector, a plastic or fibreglass support, heat-shrink tubing and sealant.
Prepare a long element of about 1470 mm and a short element of about 490 mm. Leave a little extra for tuning and account for how far the pipe seats in each fitting.
Join the elements at the bottom with the elbows and shorting bar. Aim for about 50 mm between the element centrelines after assembly.
Connect the coax shield to the long element and the centre conductor to the short one. Start about 45 mm above the shorting bar. Use adjustable contacts for tuning.
Fit a 1:1 choke at the feedpoint to suppress current on the outside of the coax shield. Choose ferrite or a choke design suitable for 145 MHz.
Mount the antenna on a non-conductive support and keep it clear of large metal objects.
Secure and weatherproof the contacts after tuning. Keep moisture away from copper-to-aluminium joints.
Measure SWR and, if available, impedance with the antenna mounted. Move both contacts together in small steps and repeat the measurement after each adjustment.
If needed, adjust the radiator length in small steps. If the design has a movable shorting bar, measure the effect of moving it separately.
Measure the finished antenna’s usable bandwidth. Pipe diameter, mounting and nearby objects all affect it.
DK7ZB’s lightweight antenna rolls up for transport. The A / B / C dimensions in his drawing are 137 cm / 42 cm / 30 mm at 145 MHz and 45.7 cm / 14 cm / 20 mm at 435 MHz.

A J-pole variant with two parallel conductors joined at the top of the radiator. Overall length is roughly 1.5 m for the 2 m band and 0.5 m for the 70 cm band. Exact dimensions depend on the materials and geometry.
A collinear design with two radiating sections and a phasing stub. Gain and radiation pattern depend on the design and installation.
A 145 MHz J-pole may show acceptable SWR near its third harmonic at 435 MHz, while its elevation pattern changes. The Open Stub J-Pole is an example designed for both bands.
A quarter-wave section of coax with a velocity factor of 0.66 is about 341 mm long at 145 MHz. Use the actual cable’s velocity factor and refine dimensions by measuring the assembled antenna.
Enter a frequency from 0.100 to 6000.000 MHz with up to six decimal places.
Enter k from 0.0001 to 1 with up to four decimal places.
The upper part of the long element forms a radiator about λ/2 long.
